title: Barry Marshall's Ulcer Theory: Keep Publishing, or Drink the Bacteria? (1984)
era: Peptic ulcer disease research, Western Australia, 1981-1994
location: Fremantle Hospital and Royal Perth Hospital, Western Australia, Australia

actors.name: Barry Marshall
actors.role: Registrar/research fellow in internal medicine at Fremantle Hospital; co-discoverer of the bacterium and the person who decided to self-infect

actors.name: J. Robin Warren
actors.role: Pathologist at Royal Perth Hospital who first identified the spiral bacteria in gastric biopsies; Marshall's research partner

actors.name: Ian Hislop
actors.role: Gastroenterology chief at Fremantle Hospital who performed Marshall's baseline and follow-up endoscopies, informally supporting the experiment

actors.name: Neil Noakes
actors.role: Microbiology laboratory scientist at Fremantle Hospital who prepared and handed Marshall the bacterial culture

actors.name: Adrienne Marshall
actors.role: Barry Marshall's wife; not told of the plan in advance, learned of it as his symptoms progressed

actors.name: David McGechie
actors.role: Chief of microbiology, Marshall's supervisor; declined Marshall's earlier informal proposal that he try the experiment himself

t0.definition: The moment in mid-1984, after a four-piglet animal-model study Marshall ran from January 1984 had failed to reproduce infection, after his and Warren's bacterial theory of gastritis and peptic ulcers had been met with open skepticism from senior colleagues and a rejected 1983 conference abstract, and after Marshall judged that a properly funded, ethics-approved, randomized human antibiotic trial was realistically years away, when Marshall must decide whether to keep pursuing that slow, conventional research and publication path, or instead drink a concentrated culture of Helicobacter pylori himself -- without submitting the plan to the hospital ethics committee -- in an attempt to fulfill Koch's postulates directly by showing the bacterium could infect and sicken a healthy person.
t0.date: Circa July 1984 (Marshall's own 2005 Nobel lecture narrates the sequence of events but does not give an exact calendar date for the day he drank the culture; secondary accounts converge on late July 1984, shortly before a July 1984 New York Times interview about the case, but no primary contemporaneous record fixes the exact date)

stakes: If Marshall was right but could not prove it quickly, patients with a treatable bacterial infection would keep receiving symptom-suppressing antacids and H2-blockers, or in severe cases surgery, for a disease a course of antibiotics could likely cure -- a real, ongoing clinical cost -- while the theory itself risked being starved of funding and academic attention. If Marshall self-infected and became seriously unwell, he risked his own health from an organism whose full disease potential in a healthy person was not established, risked being seen as having acted recklessly and outside professional norms (he was bypassing formal ethics review), and risked discrediting the theory at the moment he most needed to be believed -- all for a result that, even if it went well, would still be a single uncontrolled case, not proof that curing the infection cures ulcers.

known_at_t0.statement: Marshall and pathologist J. Robin Warren had identified spiral bacteria (later named Helicobacter pylori) in gastric biopsies and, in a roughly 100-patient study approved by the Royal Perth Hospital ethics committee, found the bacteria present in the large majority of patients with gastritis or peptic ulcers, reported in 1983 Lancet letters and a fuller 1984 Lancet paper.

A four-piglet study Marshall ran with microbiologist Stewart Goodwin starting January 1984 failed: the Helicobacter organisms he introduced did not colonize the piglets' stomachs, and the animals grew too large to continue before the study produced any usable disease model.

The dominant medical view held that peptic ulcers were caused mainly by excess stomach acid, aggravated by stress, diet, smoking, and alcohol; most gastroenterologists believed no bacterium could survive the stomach's acidic environment and treated bacteria seen in gastric tissue as harmless commensals unconnected to disease.

An abstract on the bacteria-gastritis link that Marshall and Warren submitted to the Gastroenterological Society of Australia's 1983 annual meeting was one of a small minority rejected, and Marshall later recorded open skepticism and dismissive comments from senior colleagues about the bacterial theory in the months that followed.

Marshall later wrote that a hospitalized patient with unexplained gastric bleeding tested strongly positive on his prototype antibody test for H. pylori, but was treated with transfusions, acid-blocking drugs, and antacids rather than antibiotics, and ultimately underwent a total gastrectomy -- an episode Marshall cited as showing the practical cost of the theory not yet being believed.

By the time Marshall was planning the self-experiment, he had already treated his first four Helicobacter-positive patients with a bismuth-plus-antibiotic regimen, achieving a 100% short-term cure rate on follow-up biopsy, and had shown in a simple laboratory test that bismuth was directly toxic to the bacterium.

Cimetidine (Tagamet), the leading acid-suppressing H2-blocker drug, was generating roughly US $1 billion a year for manufacturer Smith Kline & French by 1983, and the newer H2-blocker ranitidine (Zantac) went on to sell more than $3 billion a year through most of the 1980s; both drugs relieved ulcer symptoms and allowed healing but did not treat an underlying infection, so ulcers typically recurred once treatment stopped.

Marshall's application for national (NHMRC) grant funding for a randomized clinical trial of antibiotic versus standard ulcer treatment was, by his own account, received with open skepticism by the review panel, funded for only one probationary year, and giving experimental antibiotic therapy to ulcer patients ahead of stronger evidence was considered ethically premature under normal research standards given that proven treatments already existed.

Marshall later wrote that he considered submitting a self-experiment proposal to the hospital ethics committee but concluded that if it were refused he would likely proceed anyway and lose the ability to publish the results or defend his job; he judged that, because only he could truly weigh and consent to the specific unknown risk, he would proceed without formal ethics committee review, with informal, undocumented support from his endoscopist and microbiology colleagues.

When Marshall discussed the idea of a human self-infection experiment with senior colleagues beforehand, at least one (his microbiology chief, David McGechie) laughingly declined an informal invitation to try it himself, and Marshall's own later accounts describe colleagues generally regarding the plan as reckless rather than admirable.

unknown_at_t0.statement: The infection produced documented acute gastritis, confirmed by endoscopy and biopsy on day 10, but appeared to clear on its own by day 14 -- before Marshall began any antibiotic treatment -- a result Marshall has called 'a mystery to this day.'

A widely repeated popular version of the story states that Marshall's wife insisted he take antibiotics as soon as he became ill; in his own 2005 Nobel lecture, Marshall states this was not really the case -- he decided independently to end the experiment and start the antibiotic tinidazole only after the day-14 endoscopy, and notes that tinidazole alone would not have been an effective cure in any case.

It took roughly another decade of further clinical trials, epidemiological studies, and international debate -- not the self-experiment alone -- before the U.S. National Institutes of Health convened a 1994 consensus conference formally endorsing antibiotic treatment for H. pylori-associated ulcers; Australia adopted the practice considerably faster than the United States did.

Marshall and Warren were awarded the 2005 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, 21 years after the self-experiment, 'for their discovery of the bacterium Helicobacter pylori and its role in gastritis and peptic ulcer disease' -- a recognition resting on the accumulated weight of subsequent research, not the 1984 self-experiment in isolation.

Later immunological research found that widespread eradication of H. pylori in some populations is associated with rising rates of certain allergic and autoimmune conditions, leading some researchers to suggest the bacterium may also have had some immune-modulating benefit for its long-term human hosts alongside its harms -- a complication to a simple 'harmful bacterium' story that was neither knowable nor relevant to Marshall's 1984 decision.

options.label: Continue the slow, conventional research path
options.description: Keep working within normal scientific channels: publish further association studies, seek ethics-committee and grant approval for a properly randomized human antibiotic trial, and wait for accumulating data and peer opinion to shift, without attempting a direct, fast demonstration of infection causing disease in a person.
options.upside: Stayed within established research-ethics norms; avoided any personal health risk; if a rigorous randomized trial eventually succeeded, it would produce far stronger, more broadly convincing evidence than any single case could.
options.downside: Marshall judged that the funding and approval needed for a trial that would truly settle the question were themselves hard to obtain, precisely because reviewers doubted the underlying bacterial theory; in the meantime, patients kept receiving symptom-suppressing drugs or surgery for what he believed was a treatable infection, and the theory -- and his own research career -- risked being sidelined for years.
options.why_it_made_sense: This was the accepted standard for establishing a causal medical claim, and it matched what most people around Marshall actually believed was the responsible course -- when he described the self-experiment idea to colleagues beforehand, several treated it as reckless rather than admirable.
options.risk_carried: A diffuse but real risk: continued institutional inertia, more years of unnecessary antacid or surgical treatment for infected patients, and a genuine chance the theory would keep being dismissed as unproven before funding or academic interest ever arrived.

options.label: Self-experiment: drink the bacterial culture himself
options.description: Deliberately ingest a concentrated culture of H. pylori without submitting the plan to the hospital ethics committee, using himself as the only subject, in an attempt to fulfill Koch's postulates by showing the bacterium could infect a healthy person and cause disease.
options.upside: Could produce a fast, concrete, hard-to-dismiss demonstration that the bacterium caused disease in a previously healthy person, using himself as the subject so that informed consent rested with the one person able to genuinely judge the specific risk; Marshall already had a bismuth-antibiotic regimen with a track record of clearing the infection in other patients as a fallback if he became seriously unwell.
options.downside: Bypassed formal ethics review specifically because Marshall judged it would likely be refused; the actual health consequences of deliberately infecting a healthy person with this organism were not established in 1984, and even a 'successful' result would still be a single uncontrolled case, unable on its own to prove that eradicating the bacterium cures ulcers, or to rule out a worse outcome than gastritis.
options.why_it_made_sense: Marshall had exhausted the animal-model route, judged the conventional trial pathway to be realistically years away given prevailing skepticism, and believed that only his own informed self-consent could ethically authorize exposure to a risk that no ethics committee could confidently evaluate either, since nobody yet knew what ingesting the organism would do to a healthy stomach.
options.risk_carried: Unknown personal health risk from deliberate infection with an organism whose full disease potential (including a later-established association between long-term infection and gastric cancer risk) was not yet understood, plus the professional risk of having bypassed ethics review, plus the scientific risk that an N=1 result -- whatever it showed -- would still not be accepted as rigorous proof by a skeptical field.

actual_decision.decided_when: Mid-1984 (commonly reported as late July 1984), after arranging a baseline endoscopy and lining up informal support from his endoscopist and microbiology laboratory colleagues
actual_decision.stated_basis: Marshall later wrote that with no animal model, and judging a definitive human clinical trial to be both scientifically and practically out of reach in the near term, it was 'now or never' -- since he alone could give truly informed consent to the specific, unprecedented risk of swallowing the bacterium, he decided to proceed as his own subject rather than wait for institutional processes he expected would refuse or indefinitely delay the experiment.
actual_decision.constraints: He needed a healthy documented baseline (his own prior endoscopy showed a normal stomach), a way to prepare and administer a viable culture (arranged informally through microbiology colleague Neil Noakes), an endoscopist willing to perform follow-up procedures without a formal study protocol (Ian Hislop), and a fallback treatment if the infection became severe (the bismuth-antibiotic regimen already shown to work in other patients); he did not seek hospital ethics committee approval and did not tell his wife, Adrienne, in advance.

decision_quality.justification: Marshall had genuinely exhausted the animal-model route, built in real safeguards (a documented healthy baseline, an experienced endoscopist and microbiologist quietly assisting, and a bismuth-antibiotic regimen already proven to clear the infection in other patients as a fallback), and reasoned explicitly that only his own informed consent could authorize exposure to a risk no ethics committee could yet properly evaluate either. It is not rated STRONG because he deliberately bypassed ethics review rather than testing whether it would in fact be refused, did not inform his wife in advance, and accepted an open-ended, not-fully-knowable personal health risk (the organism's longer-term disease potential, later linked to gastric cancer, was not established at the time) in order to produce evidence that even in the best case would remain a single anecdote, incapable by itself of proving the more clinically important claim that eradicating the infection cures ulcers.

outcome_quality.justification: Marshall developed confirmed acute gastritis, satisfying Koch's postulates for the organism causing disease in a healthy host, and recovered fully with no lasting harm; the case drew real media attention that helped raise the theory's profile. The outcome should not be overstated, though: biopsies suggest the infection had already begun clearing on its own before Marshall started any antibiotic treatment, a result he himself calls unexplained, so part of how cleanly this resolved may reflect good luck in his individual immune response rather than a plan that reliably controlled the risk; and the self-experiment did not, by itself, end institutional resistance -- that took roughly another decade of conventional trials and epidemiology before the 1994 NIH consensus conference and the 2005 Nobel Prize.

outcome.immediate: Marshall had no symptoms for the first three days, then progressively worsening bloating, appetite loss, morning vomiting without acid, and noticeably bad breath. An endoscopy on day 10 found active gastritis and biopsies positive for spiral bacteria and inflammatory cells. A second endoscopy on day 14 found the stomach lining recovering and, unexpectedly, no detectable Helicobacter in eight biopsy samples; Marshall began the antibiotic tinidazole after this second endoscopy, on his own decision, and recovered fully.
outcome.long_term: The case drew significant media attention, including a July 1984 New York Times feature by medical writer Lawrence Altman, and was formally reported in the Medical Journal of Australia in 1985, adding a vivid, publicized data point to Marshall and Warren's growing body of evidence. It did not by itself end the field's skepticism: broad acceptance built gradually over the following decade through further clinical trials and epidemiological studies, culminating in a February 1994 NIH consensus conference that endorsed antibiotic treatment for H. pylori-associated ulcers. Marshall and Warren were jointly awarded the 2005 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the underlying discovery.

source_disagreements.topic: Whether Marshall took antibiotics 'on his wife's orders'
source_disagreements.description: Several popular retellings and some secondary science articles state that Marshall's wife, Adrienne, insisted he begin antibiotic treatment as soon as he fell ill. Marshall's own 2005 Nobel lecture explicitly states 'this was not really the case': he says he decided on his own to end the experiment and start tinidazole only after the day-14 follow-up endoscopy, by which point biopsy samples were already coming back negative for the bacterium. This repository follows Marshall's own primary account over the popularized version, and flags the popularized version as a myth worth correcting rather than treating it as settled fact.

source_disagreements.topic: Exact calendar date of the self-experiment
source_disagreements.description: Marshall's own 2005 Nobel lecture narrates the sequence of events (after the failed piglet study, before a July 1984 New York Times interview) without stating an exact calendar date for the day he drank the culture. Secondary sources converge on 'July 1984' and some add a specific claim of 'a Tuesday morning,' but no primary, contemporaneous record fixes an exact date; this repository uses 'circa July 1984' rather than asserting a specific day that isn't independently corroborated.

player_fairness.rationale: A viewer given the known_at_t0 facts (failed animal model, hostile colleagues, a real patient case where the establishment's disbelief plausibly cost a person their stomach, a grant process itself gated by skepticism of the theory) has genuine information to reason from, and the historical record shows most contemporaries around Marshall actually regarded self-infection as reckless rather than obviously wise -- this was not a fake, one-sided setup. The score is held below the strongest cases in this project because this is specifically a 'lone scientist defies the establishment and turns out to be right' story, a recognizable genre with a well-worn ending; a modern viewer primed by that genre (rather than by the specific facts given) has a real, structural advantage in guessing the historically correct answer, which is exactly the kind of hindsight-contamination risk this project is designed to avoid. This is an honest, not inflated, score.

dilemma_balance.rationale: On paper the trade-offs are genuinely two-sided (open-ended personal health risk and an ethics-committee bypass on one side; years of continued institutional inertia and ongoing patient harm on the other), and it is corroborated that contemporaries thought the self-experiment was the more extreme, not the more sensible, choice. The score is not higher because, once a viewer recognizes 'this is presented as a story about someone who mattered enough to research,' the dramatic option tends to read as the narratively 'expected' answer in this exact content format, regardless of the specific facts -- a bias this case shares with any underdog-vindicated story, but one worth being explicit about here rather than assuming it away.

context_compression.rationale: The dilemma reduces cleanly to a single, universally intuitive scene with no historical or technical prerequisite: 'nobody believes your idea, you can't test it properly any other way -- do you keep publishing papers for years, or prove it on yourself right now?' This lands in well under 10 seconds for a zero-background viewer, on par with the strongest single-image dilemmas in the curated batch.

reveal_payoff.rationale: The reveal offers real, well-sourced correctives to the flattened popular legend rather than a simple 'and then he won the Nobel Prize' close: the infection appears to have cleared on its own before any antibiotic was given (a mystery Marshall himself has never resolved), the famous 'his wife made him take the pills' detail is directly contradicted by Marshall's own account, and the self-experiment did not settle the scientific argument -- it took another decade of conventional trials and a 1994 consensus conference before the field turned, with the Nobel Prize coming 21 years later. This is a genuine intellectual payoff, though it is a quieter, more myth-correcting one than a single dramatic near-miss reveal.

production_verdict.reasoning: The underlying research is unusually well-sourced for this pilot -- Marshall's own detailed, candid 2005 Nobel lecture gives a rare first-person account of the reasoning, the ethics bypass, and the physical course of the illness, and the case delivers exceptional context_compression and a genuine, myth-correcting reveal_payoff. It is called WEAK rather than VIABLE specifically because of the concern the brief asks to be judged unsparingly: this is structurally a 'maverick defies the establishment and is vindicated' story, a well-worn narrative shape whose ending is usually guessable from the shape of the telling alone, independent of the specific facts given -- and that meta-level tell is a real fairness risk this format is meant to avoid, distinct from (and in this case outweighing) how strong the sourcing is. It remains a valuable, worthwhile data point for the stress test: it shows the format can compress and source a personal/scientific-risk decision just as cleanly as a leadership decision, but also shows that a well-documented, well-balanced-on-paper dilemma can still be undermined as a guessing game by the genre it belongs to.
